practice1.hint: The four answers are all facts pathlib already knows about the path. Splitting a hardcoded string on a slash gets the same four lines here and the wrong ones on a machine that separates folders differently.

questions.prompt: Why is "data/report.txt" written by hand a problem?
choices: Windows separates folders with a backslash, so the same string does not point at the same file everywhere
Python cannot open a path written as a string
questions.explain: The separator is an operating system detail. os.path.join and pathlib pick the right one, which is why the lesson insists on them.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a relative and an absolute path?
choices: A relative path is read from wherever the program is running; an absolute path starts at the root and means the same thing anywhere
An absolute path cannot be used with open()
questions.explain: A relative path depends on the working directory, which is exactly why the same program can find a file in one place and not another.

questions.prompt: For path = Path("data") / "report.txt", match each attribute to what it gives.
questions.explain: name is the whole filename, stem is that without the extension, suffix is the extension including the dot, and parent is the folder it sits in.

questions.prompt:
from pathlib import Path
path = Path("data") ___ "report.txt"
print(path.___)
questions.explain: pathlib overloads the slash operator to join path parts, and the right separator gets filled in for whichever system runs the code.
